status_summary: On 2026-01-22 NIH issued notice NOT-OD-26-028, effective immediately, ending use of NIH funds for research on human fetal tissue from elective abortions, in both the intramural program and extramural research (applying to proposals under solicitations issued after that date; existing awards may redirect funds to other work). This goes beyond the Mandate's request to restore an ethics advisory board review, which the notices do not mention. On 2026-01-23 NIH paused review of applications to add new human embryonic stem cell lines to its registry and opened a request for information (comments closed 2026-04-24) on replacing such cells with alternatives; the registry's existing 503 lines remain usable, so the registry has not been ended. No statutory prohibition, National Council on Bioethics, or dedicated funding plan for alternatives was found.

timeline.event: Context before the tracking window: NIH notice NOT-OD-21-111 announces that HHS is reversing its 2019 decision to send all extramural applications proposing fetal tissue from elective abortions to an ethics advisory board, and that no new board will be convened; other 2019 requirements such as donor consent remain. NOT-OD-26-028 later supersedes it.

NIH issues NOT-OD-26-028, NIH Policy on Research Involving Human Fetal Tissue: NIH funds may not be used for research on human fetal tissue from elective abortions, intramural or extramural, effective the same day. Fetal tissue from miscarriage or stillbirth remains eligible under earlier notices.

NIH news release announces the policy and says it will seek public comment on whether newer biotechnologies could reduce or replace reliance on human embryonic stem cells; it cites organoids, tissue chips, and computational methods as alternatives.

NIH issues NOT-OD-26-031: it pauses review and approval of applications to add new lines to the NIH Human Embryonic Stem Cell Registry (503 approved lines; last addition December 2023) and requests public input on where alternatives could replace human embryonic stem cells. Lines already listed remain usable in NIH-funded research.

Comment period on the human embryonic stem cell request for information (NOT-OD-26-031) closes; NIH stated that responses would be accepted through 2026-04-24. No later NIH action on embryonic stem cell funding or the registry was found.

title: End NIH funding of abortion-derived fetal tissue and embryonic stem cell research
uncertainties: Searches covered NIH Guide notices, NIH news releases, law-firm alerts, and Congress/bioethics-council terms. Not found: any NIH action on the embryonic stem cell registry after the 2026-04-24 comment deadline (a later decision could change the stage), any National Council on Bioethics, any appropriations rider or enacted statute on fetal tissue in the 119th Congress, or any lawsuit against the policy. The Ropes & Gray alert is dated by month only (January 2026, first of month used). Checks on 2026-10-14: the NIH Office of Science Policy stem cell policy page (footer shows last updated June 2026; page metadata 2026-06-29) still describes the registry pause under NOT-OD-26-031 and lists no notice after April 2026. NIH's FY2026 legislative mandates notice (2026-03-18) lists the human embryo research funding ban in the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 (Public Law 119-75, signed 2026-02-03) and does not list a fetal tissue provision, so no enacted statutory fetal tissue prohibition was found for FY2026. A House Appropriations Committee release of 2025-09-02 on the FY2026 Labor-HHS subcommittee markup quotes the subcommittee chairman as saying the bill ensures that tax dollars do not support research using fetal tissue from an abortion, but that bill text was not read and was not shown enacted. The House FY2027 Labor-HHS bill was approved by the House Appropriations Committee on 2026-06-09 (34 to 28, per the committee's release, which does not mention fetal tissue); its bill text was not checked for fetal tissue provisions. Searches for lawsuits, rescissions or registry decisions after 2026-04-24 returned none; litigation might not appear in such results.
